pages.title: Ken Page on Discouragement Fatigue and the Wave of Distancing
pages.short_answer: On episode 106 of Christina Weber's podcast, psychotherapist Ken Page, author of Deeper Dating, names the two patterns that most derail people looking for love: discouragement fatigue and the wave of distancing. His fix is to measure progress by whether you're becoming more self-treasuring, vulnerable, and discriminating, and to keep asking one question: does my soul feel safe with this person?
pages.meta_description: Ken Page, author of Deeper Dating, on discouragement fatigue, the wave of distancing, and the one question to date by. Key ideas and quotes from episode 106.
pages.content_html:
Ken Page, LCSW, is a psychotherapist, the author of Deeper Dating, host of the Deeper Dating Podcast, and a member of WeDeepen's faculty. Christina Weber calls him one of her mentors in love: "I go to him all the time when I need relationship advice." In episode 106 of her podcast, he named the two patterns he sees derail people looking for love most often, and what to do about each. This guide sums up that conversation. Quotes are from the episode transcript, lightly edited for readability.

Discouragement fatigue

Ken once asked everyone on his email list where they get most stuck in dating. More than a hundred people answered, and he sent each a personal voice message back. One woman named the problem in two words: discouragement fatigue.

It's the slow wear of trying again and again. Dating relationships that don't work. Long-term relationships that end in heartbreak. What Ken calls "the culture of unkindness" in so much of the dating world, the swipe apps, and the disappointment of doing it all over again. It hits hardest after what he calls stepping-stone relationships: you've done the inner work, you meet someone who seems different, and it ends the same way, only worse, "because their hopes were higher."

His answer isn't to try harder. It's to change what you measure. "The degree to which you uplevel the way you search for love is really the degree to which you're going to uplevel the kind of person you're going to meet." In place of "Did this one work out?", he offers three questions:

  • Am I becoming more self-treasuring?
  • Am I becoming more vulnerable?
  • Am I becoming more discriminating?

"If the answers to those questions are yes, you are on the right path." That, he says, is how you find light in the middle of the tunnel, not just at the end of it.

The wave of distancing

The second pattern is the one Ken calls "the worst saboteur of healthy new love that exists." If you're used to people who are not quite available, then the moment you meet someone who is truly present, your attraction can suddenly drop. "All of a sudden you notice their nose hair. You notice that their laugh irritates you. You notice that your sexual desire diminishes." In his experience, between a third and a half of all people who date go through it, and "nobody's taught to deal with it."

His guidance: expect it, and don't let it make the decision for you. He borrows a line from Marianne Williamson: "both feet in until both feet out." With someone truly available, he says, "you will be afraid, you will be nervous, you'll want to escape," but "it passes if you let the love deepen and it's the right person."

The one question to date by

Attraction matters, Ken says, but it shouldn't come first. His central question: "Does my soul feel safe with this person? Frame your entire search for love around that question and watch what changes." When your soul feels safe with someone who is present, available, and mutually attracted, "that's the happiness you could glide on almost forever."

He's also direct about two things that stall progress no matter how much inner work you've done: active addiction, and serious psychiatric conditions that haven't been stabilized. Get help with those first, he says, or "you're going to tread the same ground again and again."

Your scariest ask is your core gift

Christina shared a story from her own love life. Ken had urged her to ask a partner a question she was afraid to ask. She resisted all evening, then asked. Whatever the answer, the relief was immediate, and the relationship got more honest.

Ken's reading of that moment is the heart of his Deeper Dating approach, which centers on naming and honoring your core gifts: "The things we're most afraid to share and most afraid to ask for not only are often the most important things, they are our deepest core gifts." And: "The parts of ourselves we leave behind in order to get love or approval are the parts of ourselves we need to champion and reclaim in order to really find healthy love."

Christina put the flip side plainly: "The true feeling of abandonment, I've found, is when I abandon myself."

How this fits WeDeepen's approach

Ken's work lines up closely with WeDeepen's premise that love is a trainable skill. The Four Pillars say the same thing in different words: growth comes first, with no attachment to outcome; you own your own experience; and all feelings are welcome, including the fear that shows up when someone good arrives. Both Ken and Christina stress support: nobody gets better at love alone. That's why WeDeepen runs a weekly live session and community and Love Immersion retreats in Austin. To practice with others, join the membership. Come play with us.

FAQ

Who is Ken Page?

Ken Page, LCSW, is a psychotherapist, the author of Deeper Dating, host of the Deeper Dating Podcast, and a member of WeDeepen's faculty.

What is discouragement fatigue?

It's the exhaustion that builds from repeated dating disappointments, breakups, and unkindness, a term one of Ken Page's readers coined. He suggests measuring progress by whether you're becoming more self-treasuring, vulnerable, and discriminating, not by whether each relationship lasts.

What is the wave of distancing?

Ken Page's term for losing attraction or wanting to escape just as you meet someone truly available. He estimates it affects between a third and a half of people who date, and says it usually passes if you stay present and the person is right for you.

What question does Ken Page recommend asking when dating?

"Does my soul feel safe with this person?" He suggests framing your whole search for love around it, alongside attraction.

Where can I listen to the full episode?

Episode 106 is on the WeDeepen podcast page, Apple Podcasts, and YouTube.

pages.title: Kimi Inch on Conscious Kink: Safety, Play, and Desire
pages.short_answer: On episode 108 of Christina Weber's podcast, Austin somatic therapist Kimi Inch, founder of &More, explains conscious kink as consensual, creative play built on attunement. Her keys: a regulated nervous system comes before pleasure, every exercise is an invitation you can decline, and desire is learned in the body, not from a book. Christina shares what she learned at Kimi's four-day immersion.
pages.meta_description: Kimi Inch on conscious kink: nervous-system safety, consent as invitation, and learning the Erotic Blueprints in your body. Key ideas from episode 108.
pages.content_html:
Kimi Inch is a somatic therapist, Core Energetics practitioner, and founder of &More, an erotic leadership brand based in Austin. She is also on WeDeepen's faculty. In episode 108 of Christina Weber's podcast, recorded at Kimi's Austin home, the two walked through Something More, Kimi's four-day immersion in conscious kink, which Christina had just finished. This guide sums up what they said about safety, play, and learning desire in your body instead of from a book. Quotes are from the episode transcript, lightly edited for readability.

Kink is play, not a stereotype

Many people say "I'm not kinky." Christina's follow-up question: do you like to play? To her, kink is "novel, it's play, it's experimenting with what's possible and feeling into my emotions."

Kimi says it makes sense that people feel nervous, because the media mostly shows "this really cliche, dark, heavy, intense" picture. What she wants to bring forward is "imagination and creativity." Her playful rewrite of the stereotype: "Instead of blood, sweat, and tears, can't we just do grace and elegance instead?"

Kink names, like the one Christina took on this year, "Your Majesty," are part of the play. Kimi describes them as one instrument in an inner symphony: "Sometimes you want to give that violin a solo."

Safety starts in the nervous system

Christina asked what someone should do if they crave deeper intimacy but don't yet feel safe enough to explore it. Kimi's answer was about the body, not technique. "If we are struggling to keep a regulated nervous system, it's really hard for us to step into our pleasure and to be in deep connection and intimacy with another."

The fix is gradual exposure in a well-held setting, whether that's a therapist, a coach, or "a well-organized, conscious event where people can hold a container." Each time you're vulnerable and nothing bad happens, your nervous system learns, "I can be heard, and people can be present with me, and I won't be judged or rejected or shamed." That, she says, "opens you up to infinite possibility around pleasure and relational experiences."

Christina sees herself as proof. After years of practices like eye gazing in Tantra and connection workshops, what once felt edgy now feels easy, and each layer she goes deeper shows her a new one.

Everything is an invitation

Kimi opens every immersion with one agreement: "Everything is just a series of invitations. There's no expectation, there's no demand." You choose your own pace, and you can stop or change your mind at any time. She also asks the group to "celebrate everything," including trying an exercise for five seconds and deciding it isn't for you.

She pushes back on the idea that erotic spaces require you to be cool and polished: "We really want to encourage realness and rawness and vulnerability over this performance sort of sexy image." Christina noted that about half the group came as couples and half were currently single, and that the space honored both: "We're relationshipping in community."

Learning desire in the body

Day two of Something More centered on the Erotic Blueprints, a framework created by sex educator Jaiya that sorts arousal styles into five types: Energetic, Sensual, Sexual, Kinky, and Shapeshifter. Blueprint coach Kayce Neill taught the framework, and Kimi built a hands-on exercise for each type.

Her reason is simple: "I can attribute every successful erotic encounter with the ability of how attuned me and my partner are to ourselves and to each other." Reading about attunement isn't the same as feeling it. "Most of the time people just don't know what's possible in their lives until they actually have an experience of it. It's all theory until then."

Christina's own results changed with experience. Her first quiz months earlier put her in one type, and she felt boxed in. After the immersion she retook it and came out a Shapeshifter, which felt right. She now sees a primary blueprint as "a gateway into all of the others." Day three moved into rope work (shibari) and impact play, taught by professionals and framed as ways to practice surrender, leading, and trust.

Why this matters for your love life

Christina's point running through the episode: sex education stops at age 13, and adults rarely get a second chance. "Relationship education is something that is never ending and unfolding." That's WeDeepen's premise too. Love is a trainable skill, all feelings are welcome, and you own your own experience at every step. Practice works best repeated over time, not crammed into one weekend. WeDeepen's membership gives you a weekly live session and a community to keep practicing in, and Love Immersion retreats in Austin offer an in-person reset. Join the membership. Come play with us.

FAQ

Who is Kimi Inch?

Kimi Inch is an Austin-based somatic therapist, Core Energetics practitioner, and founder of &More, who teaches conscious kink and erotic leadership. She is on WeDeepen's faculty.

What is conscious kink?

As Kimi Inch describes it, conscious kink is consensual erotic play built on attunement, care, and choice, where every activity is an invitation you can accept, decline, or stop at any time.

What are the five Erotic Blueprint types?

Energetic, Sensual, Sexual, Kinky, and Shapeshifter. The framework was created by Jaiya. Most people are a mix of all five, with one or two leading.

Do you need a partner to explore this kind of work?

No. In the immersion Christina attended, about half the participants came as couples and half were currently single.

Where can I listen to the full episode?

Episode 108 is on the WeDeepen podcast page, Apple Podcasts, and YouTube. For Kimi's background, listen to episode 99, Beyond the Whip.

pages.title: Dilia Jelen on Loving Again After Divorce
pages.short_answer: On episode 62 of Christina Weber's podcast, Dilia Jelen describes a divorce that left her starting over from zero and took about three years to heal. Her lessons for loving again: be completely transparent, including about money; don't make a new relationship carry the fears of the old one; stay open to someone you'd once have ruled out; and build an equal, supportive love where neither person tries to control the other.
pages.meta_description: Dilia Jelen on healing after divorce and loving again: full transparency, leaving old fears behind, and equal, supportive love. Key ideas from episode 62.
pages.content_html:
Dilia Jelen has spent more than a decade working with children in orphanages and with survivors of abuse and trafficking, for eight years as a full-time volunteer across 29 countries. She is also one of Christina Weber's oldest friends: they met around the first Feminine Weapon Day, the annual benefit Christina founded for children's education, art, and healing programs. In episode 62 of Christina's podcast, Dilia talked openly about a divorce that took everything she knew, the three years it took to heal, and the very different love she built afterward. This guide sums up what she learned. Quotes are from the episode transcript, lightly edited for readability.

Divorce changes you, even a good one

Dilia's divorce left her starting over financially from zero. The one thing she kept was the apartment she'd had for 17 years. The work she loved, which she had done alongside her husband, ended with the marriage. It happened as the pandemic arrived, so she did what many people do: she got very quiet.

She doesn't sugarcoat it. "For those of you who have ever been through divorce, even if you have the most healthy divorce, it is something that just shifts you and changes you in a way that you can't really ever prepare for." For her, "it took me a good three years to heal completely."

She also made a choice about timing. She didn't want to bring what she called her "broken self" to the children she serves. "I think it's really important for us who are aware and conscious to do all the work that we possibly can on ourselves to get ourselves whole." The same instinct shaped how she came back to love.

Transparency is not optional

The biggest lesson Dilia took from her first marriage was about honesty. She wants people to know "how important it is to be completely transparent in relationship, and honest a hundred percent, and that there's no way a relationship can win if those things aren't there."

In her marriage, money was never discussed. Christina named the pattern she sees often, especially in second relationships where one partner has a lot to lose: "We're so scared to lose it that we then withhold, and we're secretive." Dilia agreed, and added that the fear is usually invented. "A lot of the time it's just something we create in our head." No amount of therapy helps, she said, if you don't get out of your own way: "Your fear will always take you over, and the beauty in your life will always go away."

In her new marriage, money talk came early and plainly. When her partner moved to New York to try life in her world, she covered them both for a couple of months until his work picked up. They had less than she'd had before, and it felt like more. "It's just so important to really come together and to just share, and to become a team with your partner."

Don't bring the old relationship into the new one

Dilia met her now-husband a few months after she separated. She wasn't looking. "When we met I was totally broken, and I said no to any kind of relationship." They talked on the phone for hours a day as friends. When he proposed early, she told him she couldn't marry him, and later she let him go entirely while she went through a very hard stretch. She called him again about a year later, healthier, and it was obvious what they had.

What she did differently was refuse to make the new relationship pay for the old one. "I could have had all these fears of everything I'd been through. I chose to not bring my past into this beautiful, fresh, new relationship. I wanted it to have its own life and its own discovery."

Her warning for anyone dating again after a long relationship: "When we get hurt and we live really hard things, we tend to bring a lot of our lessons with us. But sometimes they don't serve us. Sometimes they hinder us, and they might keep us from the relationship that we should be in."

Stay open to the person you'd have ruled out

Her husband is 14 years younger than she is. At first, she says, "my mind would never have entertained that." What changed her mind was who he was: educated, with several careers, taking care of his family, "this whole, complete person." Having dated across ages, cultures, and industries, her conclusion is simple: "Sure, there are some stereotypes, but the fact of the matter is, we are all individuals."

For anyone back on the dating market after years away, that's a useful nudge. The rules you made at 25 about who fits may not be the ones that serve you now.

Back-to-back love

Dilia had always been the caretaker in her relationships, "the nurse for every partner I've ever had." In this one she is cared for too, and the balance feels equal. She described it with an image she credits to Alejandro Jodorowsky: a healthy love doesn't have to be face to face and all-consuming. It can be two people sitting back to back, supporting each other, connected, and still living their own lives. "A divine love doesn't need to change anything about the other. It just loves." Their rule, she said: "It is never to control or take one another over. It's always just to support."

And she wants people who've been hurt to hear this: "All human beings, even if we haven't gotten it right in relationships in the past, we all deserve this kind of love, this equal, supportive love."

How this fits WeDeepen's approach

Dilia's story lines up with WeDeepen's premise that love is a trainable skill, and with the Four Pillars: you own your own experience, all feelings are welcome, and growth comes first. Taking time to heal, choosing honesty about money and fear, and refusing to let the past write the next chapter are all things you can practice. For more on starting again, read how to start dating again after divorce. If you're back in the dating world after a long relationship, WeDeepen's membership for dating again gives you live sessions with relationship experts and a community to practice with, starting with a free trial. You can also meet people in person at Love Immersion in Austin. Come play with us.

FAQ

Who is Dilia Jelen?

Dilia Jelen works with children in orphanages and with survivors of abuse and trafficking around the world, and is a longtime friend of WeDeepen founder Christina Weber and of Feminine Weapon Day.

How long did it take Dilia to heal after her divorce?

About three years, she said. She describes divorce, even a healthy one, as something that changes you in ways you can't prepare for.

What was her biggest lesson from her first marriage?

Complete transparency, including about money. In her view, a relationship can't work without full honesty, and fear of loss is what makes people withhold.

How did she approach her new relationship differently?

She chose not to bring her past fears into it, talked openly about finances, and treated her partner as a teammate. She also stayed open to someone she would once have ruled out.

Where can I listen to the full episode?

Episode 62 is on the WeDeepen podcast page, Apple Podcasts, and YouTube.

pages.title: Roxy Ruse on Why Desire Fades: Safety, Trust and Repair
pages.short_answer: On episode 142 of Christina Weber's podcast, WeDeepen's Roxy Ruse explains why desire faded in her 15-year marriage. After ruling out medical causes, she found the cause was a lost sense of safety and trust, because hurts went unrepaired. Her advice: treat repair as a practice, slow down and stay present in the discomfort, and make it safe for your partner to be fully themselves.
pages.meta_description: Why does desire fade in a long relationship? Roxy Ruse on safety, trust, and the repair that keeps desire alive. Key ideas and quotes from episode 142.
pages.content_html:
Roxy Ruse is WeDeepen's community manager and events coordinator. She recorded episode 142 of Christina Weber's podcast on her third day on the job. She was married for about 15 years, and she and her former husband now co-parent their children. When Christina asked what happened to desire in that marriage, Roxy gave one of the clearest answers we've heard: it wasn't hormones, and it wasn't time. It was safety, trust, and repair. This guide sums up that part of the conversation. Quotes are from the episode transcript, lightly edited for readability.

She did all the things

Like a lot of people in long relationships, Roxy reached a point where she couldn't understand why her desire for her partner had gone. "I did all the things. I went to the therapist. I went to the doctor. I went to the hormone doctor. I was like, what is going on with me that I can't actually have this, even emotional connection, or this physical desire for this person that I've been with, that I should be so connected to?"

Checking the physical side first is sensible, and worth doing. But for Roxy the answer wasn't there. "What personally impacted me with desire was a sense of safety and a lack of trust."

Desire fades in the space where repair should be

It took her a long time to see where the lack of safety came from. "My sense of safety and my lack of trust was due to a lack of desire to repair within the relationship."

She thinks this is one of the hardest things a couple can face: one person sees that something needs repairing, and the other doesn't. "When one person is not willing to see, or willing to even attempt to understand or feel that maybe repair needs to happen in some way, shape or form, then that creates space. And in that space, the desire ends up fading."

That's a different picture from the usual story that desire simply wears out. In Roxy's telling, desire faded because hurts kept going unrepaired, and each one left a little more distance.

Repair is a practice nobody taught us

Christina asked what someone in a relationship right now could do to start repairing. Roxy's first answer: "We are not taught how to do that." She never saw repair modeled growing up. "I never received repair as a child. So I didn't know what it felt like."

Christina pointed out why it's so hard in the moment: when a rupture happens and your nervous system is triggered, you can't reach for the tools you know. The answer is repetition. Inside WeDeepen, members had just had a Love Mastermind on nonviolent communication and kept practicing it together afterward. Roxy's advice: find a repair method that "feels good to your body," then "practice, practice in community, practice with your friends. I practice with my kids."

Whatever the method, she says the core is the same: come back to yourself, connect, and slow down. "Repair does require you to slow down and be present with another person in the uncomfortable."

Be unoffendable, and let it be messy

Most people avoid repair because the conversation is uncomfortable and they're afraid of saying it wrong. Christina shared a practice she uses in her relationships and at WeDeepen: being unoffendable. "When I'm unoffendable, then it gives spaciousness for somebody else to be messy with their words for a moment, and then we can come back to alignment."

What both of them are listening for is care, more than perfect wording. "You can really sense energetically when somebody's heart or energy, when they really care," Christina said. That's what most of us want from a partner: proof that our experience matters to them.

Make it safe to be fully yourself

Roxy carried the lesson into her current relationship, with a partner of two and a half years. Her intention now: "that the other person always feels like they can be who they want to be with me, or that they feel like they can share whatever they want to share with me."

She has felt what that does from the other side. Her partner gave her "a space in their world to be my complete honest, silly, crazy, annoying, neurotic self," and in that safety she was able to rewrite old stories about not being good enough, not being able to use her voice, and her desires being "unacceptable, not good enough, weird." Safety, in her experience, is what lets desire come out of hiding.

Safe is not the same as settled

Christina added a twist from her own love life. A friend looked at a man Christina had a mild crush on and said he looked safe, too safe, like settling. When the friend showed her someone else, Christina felt more butterflies. Roxy named it "fear of the uncomfortable." The takeaway for long relationships: safety and trust are the foundation, but desire also needs a little aliveness and risk. Both matter.

How this fits WeDeepen's approach

Christina believes community is your third: the people who help a couple stay in love, the way guests at a wedding promise to. WeDeepen exists so couples have that third and a place to practice. Love is a trainable skill, and repair is one of the most important parts of it. For the research on keeping desire alive, read how to keep desire alive in a long-term relationship, and to decide what kind of help fits, see couples coaching vs. couples therapy. If you're in a long relationship that has gone flat, WeDeepen's membership for couples and long relationships gives you weekly live sessions with relationship experts, including Love Masterminds like the one on nonviolent communication, starting with a free trial. Come play with us.

FAQ

Who is Roxy Ruse?

Roxy Ruse is WeDeepen's community manager and events coordinator, based in Austin. She has hosted community events for years and has studied love and relationships for at least five.

Why does desire fade in a long relationship, according to Roxy?

In her experience, it faded because of a lost sense of safety and trust, which came from hurts that were never repaired. She ruled out medical causes first, which is worth doing.

What is repair in a relationship?

Repair is how a couple comes back together after a rupture: slowing down, being present in the discomfort, and showing the other person that their experience matters. Nonviolent communication is one method.

How do you get better at repair?

Practice it often, with your partner, your friends, your kids, and in community, so the tools are there when your nervous system is triggered.

Where can I listen to the full episode?

Episode 142 is on the WeDeepen podcast page, Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and YouTube.

Sources

  • Spotify: DWC 142

pages.title: Derek Hart on How Couples Repair: Say What's Hurting
pages.short_answer: On episode 29 of Christina Weber's podcast, couples coach Derek Hart explains that most struggling couples aren't incompatible; their communication stopped working years ago. Repeated fights are about the bond feeling at risk, not the topic. His approach: slow down, say the one sentence that's been held in, and let your partner take it in. Three to five of those moments, he says, can make a couple feel secure again.
pages.meta_description: Couples coach Derek Hart on why couples fight about their bond, not the topic, and how to repair by saying what's hurting. Key ideas from episode 29.
keywords: couples fighting about the same thing
pages.content_html:
Derek Hart is a couples coach who has worked with couples for more than three decades. He found the work after trying seven times to leave a relationship that wasn't good for him, and spending years in Co-Dependents Anonymous figuring out "how do people relate, how do they connect, what is really going on here." Christina Weber sat down with him in Miami after he gave the keynote at the first RelateFest. In episode 29 of her podcast, he explained how he helps couples on the edge of breaking up feel close again. This guide sums up that conversation. Quotes are from the episode transcript, lightly edited for readability.

Incompatible, or just stuck?

When couples arrive asking whether they should stay together, Derek's first question is whether they have a real incompatibility. One person wanting to sail the world and the other wanting a farm is one. But that's rare. "Couples usually don't actually have an incompatibility. What they have is communication that hasn't worked, often for years, sometimes for decades."

Sometimes, after real work, it turns out one partner doesn't want the depth the other wants. That is an incompatibility, and he treats it as one. His stated goal with every couple is honest about both outcomes: "to get closer as soon as possible, or to break up as soon as possible."

Most couples ask for help too late

Derek once tried to estimate how many couples ever see a couples counselor. Working from the number of licensed counselors in a city, how much of their practice is couples, and the local population, he landed at roughly one in 400. That's his own back-of-the-envelope figure, not a published study, but it matches what he sees: "They come very, very late in the game." By then the pain is with them all day, and it affects their kids, their friendships, and their work.

His advice runs the other way. "If you were brilliant enough to come to see a marriage counselor in the first three weeks of your relationship, because you both had things from the past that snuck up and tripped you up, that would be absolutely brilliant." Before that, he suggests reading good books on relationships, naming Sue Johnson's Hold Me Tight, and getting honest about your own pattern. In his experience, everyone does one of a few things: "you hide, you run away, or you blame, or you build up resentment."

The sentence that opens everything

Derek doesn't need a couple's history to start. He watches them talk about in-laws, money, the house, the kids, and looks for what he calls emotional signals. "Every couple that comes has a sentence that they could say to the other that would open up everything."

He gave an example. He slows the couple down, has them make eye contact, and helps one partner say the thing underneath the complaints, something like: "I remember how it used to be when we first connected, and I miss that so much. Where's the person that was my best friend?" Often she starts crying, because that's what has been held in.

Then her partner gets defensive, because all he hears is that he's doing it wrong again. So Derek helps him reveal what's under that: "I feel blamed. I feel like I can never get it right with you." Both people are hurting, both are bracing, and neither has said it. Within the first 15 or 20 minutes, couples often realize "this is what I've needed to say for five years."

You're never fighting about dinner

This may be the most useful idea in the episode. When a couple starts the same argument they've had a thousand times, "they are not talking about the topic they think they're talking about. They are talking about their bond being in peril, every single time." Even a fight over Chinese or Italian food, he says, is really: "I don't feel loved." "Well, I don't either."

That moment, the familiar argument starting up, is the signal to stop arguing the topic and switch to vulnerability and attunement. Couples who can't solve problems, he says, usually can't because the bond feels unsafe. "We need to make their bond secure so that they can solve their own problems."

Vulnerability, then attunement

Derek separates the two. Vulnerability is "dropping in to the thing that I am scared about" and saying it: I'm scared, I'm confused, when you leave I feel abandoned. Attunement is what happens next, often before a word is spoken back. "The eye contact between the two, before the other person even responds, that's emotional attunement." Does the listener see that this was hard to say, and that it matters?

His measure of progress is specific. When a couple has "somewhere between three and five actual bonding moments in front of me, where they feel deeply how they've affected the other person, and the other person receives that and feels gotten," and then another 10 to 12 on their own, he says they're securely reattached.

What men want most

Christina asked what he sees men wanting. His answer: the criticism usually starts early, men skip over how much it hurts, and resentment builds without either partner noticing. But underneath, "he just wants to figure out how to make her happy." Even after years of resentment, "if he does something right in the session with me and she likes it and smiles, he's in heaven immediately."

FAQ

Who is Derek Hart?

Derek Hart is a couples coach with more than 30 years of experience helping couples on the edge of breaking up. He gave the keynote at the first RelateFest in Miami.

How does Derek Hart tell if a couple is incompatible?

He asks whether the problem is a true incompatibility, like wanting completely different lives, or communication that hasn't worked for years. In his experience it's usually the second.

What are couples really fighting about?

According to Derek, a familiar argument is almost always about the bond feeling at risk, not the topic. That's the moment to slow down and share what's underneath.

How many sessions does it take?

He often talks about the first eight hours, either weekly sessions or an intensive, and describes a couple as reattached after three to five bonding moments in session and 10 to 12 at home.
